study.title: Psalm 94 The God who sees oppression and sustains his
study.overview: Psalm 94 is an intense supplication for God to intervene against the wicked and at the same time a source of comfort for the persecuted people. The psalmist begins by crying out to the God of righteousness to manifest himself against the arrogant who crush the weak, denying divine attention to what they do. Then confront the foolishness of those who imagine that God does not see or judge, and shows that the Lord disciplines, teaches and does not abandon his people. In the final part, the poem goes from the lament to trust: the psalmist himself reports the help he received, denounces the oppressive power that makes unjust laws and concludes with the certainty that God will cause their own evil to fall.

outline.title: Clamor for justice against the oppressors
outline.explanation: The psalmist invokes the Lord as God of vengeances and Judge of the earth, asking that he rise up against the arrogant. He describes the violence of the wicked against the people of God, especially against the vulnerable, and denounces their false security, who think that God does not see or pay attention.

outline.title: Rebuke the fools and promise of support to God's people
outline.explanation: Here the psalm confronts the folly of those who suppose that the Creator does not hear, does not see and does not correct. Then declare the disciplined man blessed by God and instructed by his Law, because the Lord will not forsake his people and make judgment and righteousness prevail.

outline.title: Personal experience of help and certainty of the final judgment
outline.explanation: The psalmist reports his own dependence on the Lord when he felt almost falling and burdened by worries. He contrasts the throne of wickedness with the refuge he found in God and ends by stating that the Lord will repay the wicked with his own wickedness.

study.context: The notes describe this psalm as an appeal to divine justice in the midst of the oppression of the people of God. Matthew Henry understands him as an expression of the situation of the persecuted church, combining accusation against oppressors and comfort to the persecuted. Adam Clarke suggests that psalm may have emerged as a prayer of captives for deliverance, although this historical identification is presented by him as likely, not certain. The notes also note that the poem alternates community labying, confrontation with the wicked and personal trust in divine help.
study.theology: The psalm states that God is not indifferent to unrighteousness: he is Judge of the earth and the God to whom retribution belongs. The language of "revenge" must be read, according to Adam Clarke, as retributive justice, that is, to give each one what it fits, and not as an uncontrolled passion. The text also teaches that divine discipline does not contradict the love of God; on the contrary, it is part of his wise instruction and his care for his own. There is still a theology of providence: the wicked may seem to triumph, but their apparent security is illusory, for the Lord knows thoughts, sees actions, sustains the righteous in his weakness and will cause their own wickedness to fall upon the wicked. For an evangelical reading, this harmonizes with the confidence that God judges with righteousness and preserves those who belong to him, even in the midst of affliction.

scholarViews.insight: The Psalm brings together community lament and individual expression of pain, but it also shows the comfort and stability of the protection of the Lord.
The promises of God transform discipline into bliss, for the Lord corrects his people for his good.
The avenging attributed to the Lord is described as retributive justice, not as vengeful passion; he gives each one what is due to him.

questions: How does this psalm correct the idea that injustice goes unnoticed by God?
How can God's discipline be understood as a sign of care and not abandonment?
In what practical situations can we repeat the psalmist's confidence that the Lord is refuge when everything seems to slip?
study.practice: Take to God, in honest prayer, the situation of injustice that most anguish, without trying to disguise the pain. At the same time, examine whether there is any area in which you have treated God's discipline as weight without realizing that it can be loving instruction. Finally, practice active trust: instead of returning evil for evil, handing over the cause to the Lord and proceeding doing what is right, remembering that he sees, sustains and judges with justice.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not allow to safely confirm a specific historical scenario for the psalm; the suggestion of a context of captivity in Babylon appears only as Adam Clarke's hypothesis. It is also not possible to determine the human author or the exact date. Where the text and commentators differ in tone, this study preserves the main reading of the psalm: a prayer for justice and a comfort for the persecuted people.
